---
title: "CPI Components"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(fbi)
library(psych)
library(kableExtra)
```

FRED-MD (McCracken and Ng) publishes three Consumer Price Index subcomponents we look at here:

- `CPIAPPSL`: Apparel
- `CPITRNSL`: Transportation
- `CPIMEDSL`: Medical Care

These are different market baskets with different price drivers: apparel tracks import costs and retail markdowns, transportation is dominated by energy prices, medical care is shaped by insurance and health policy. There is no direct mechanism linking them month to month. But all three are nominal price indices, so all three trend upward for the same reason: aggregate inflation. That shared trend is exactly the kind of confound ECE is built to strip out, which makes this a good complement to `copy-number-variation.qmd`: instead of physically unrelated genomic probes sharing an instrument-calibration drift, these are economically unrelated goods sharing a decades-long inflation drift. We test the joint null that the 3x3 correlation matrix is diagonal.

```{R cpi-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

fred_data <- fredmd(
  "../data/real-data/FRED-2026-05.csv",
  date_start = NULL, date_end = NULL, transform = FALSE
) |> as_tibble()

X_data <- fred_data |>
  select(date, CPIAPPSL, CPITRNSL, CPIMEDSL) |>
  drop_na() |>
  rename(
    `Apparel`        = CPIAPPSL,
    `Transportation` = CPITRNSL,
    `Medical Care`   = CPIMEDSL
  )

X_mat   <- as.matrix(X_data[, -1])
X_seg   <- segment_mean(X_mat, penalty = "BIC")
X_resid <- X_mat - X_seg
```

## Diagnostics

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R cpi-plot-raw}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-cpi-components
#| fig-cap: "CPI subcomponents, monthly levels, 1959-2026. Thick lines show the segmented mean."
#| fig-height: 7

X <- bind_cols(
  date = X_data$date, X_data[, -1],
  as.data.frame(X_seg) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_segment"))
)

X |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type     = if_else(str_ends(series, "_segment"), "Segmented", "Raw"),
    category = str_remove(series, "_segment$")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = category, group = series)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = type)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Raw = 0.4, Segmented = 1.0), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "CPI Subcomponents", x = NULL, y = "Index level", color = "Category",
    caption = "Source: FRED-MD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

All three climb steadily for six decades. Transportation is the most volatile, tracking energy price shocks (2008, 2021-2022); Medical Care is the smoothest, climbing almost without pause.

## Trend

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Naive

Same 3x3 matrix layout as the Mean-Shift-Invariant tab: diagonal is each series' own rolling-mean-removed variance, upper triangle is the naive pairwise covariance term, lower triangle blank.

```{R cpi-trend-naive}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)

R <- apply(X_mat, 2, function(col) col - rolling_mean(col, window))
idx_p <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)

naive_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_p)), function(k) {
  i <- idx_p[1, k]
  j <- idx_p[2, k]
  s <- R[, i] * R[, j]
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
naive_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- R[, i] * R[, i]
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
naive_terms_dat <- bind_rows(naive_cov_dat, naive_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn)) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), global = mean(raw, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(naive_terms_dat, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "naive term (covariance / variance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Mean-Shift-Invariant

`plot_ece_terms()`'s underlying term, `lag_term()`, compares each point against its two predecessors using a circular shift (`rotate()`). On a series that trends for 60+ years without ever cycling back, the last couple of points wrap around and get compared against the 1959 starting level, producing a huge artificial spike that swamps every other point on the y-axis. Laid out as a 3x3 matrix, same row/column convention as the Correlation tables below: the diagonal is each series' own variance term (`lag_term(X[,i], X[,i])`), the upper triangle is the pairwise covariance term, and the lower triangle is left blank since it's redundant with the upper triangle.

```{R cpi-trend-ece-data}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
idx    <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)

ece_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
ece_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
ece_terms_dat <- bind_rows(ece_cov_dat, ece_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn))
```

```{R cpi-trend-ece}
#| echo: false

ece_terms_trend <- ece_terms_dat |>
  filter(t > 2, t < n - 1) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), global = mean(raw)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ece_terms_trend, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "ECE term (covariance / variance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The large excursion around 2021 in all three panels is the COVID-era inflation shock, not an artifact. The boundary artifact is a separate, smaller-in-count but larger-in-magnitude problem, and the plot above still excludes it (it excludes the display only — every `ece.test()` p-value elsewhere in this chapter is computed on the full, untrimmed series). The histogram below shows the *full*, untrimmed term distribution, including those boundary points, on the same 3x3 row/column layout (diagonal = variance term, upper triangle = covariance term), so its impact is visible directly instead of trimmed away.

```{R cpi-trend-hist}
#| echo: false

ece_terms_summary <- ece_terms_dat |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(raw), median = median(raw), .groups = "drop")

ece_terms_trimmed <- ece_terms_dat |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  filter(raw > quantile(raw, 0.005), raw < quantile(raw, 0.995)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ece_terms_trimmed, aes(x = raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_summary, aes(xintercept = mean), color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_summary, aes(xintercept = median), color = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "ECE term value (middle 99%)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Almost every observation sits in a single bar near zero; the x-axis has to stretch out to several hundred to fit one or two boundary points per panel, and those same one or two points are what `bs_multiplier_test` and `bs_parametric_test` build their statistics from internally (both call `ece_terms(X)` on this exact, untrimmed data). The mean (dashed red) and median (dashed orange) both sit essentially on top of zero in every panel — the boundary points don't move the center of the distribution much, but they do move `sum(s_t^2)`, which is what the bootstrap null variance is built from. A handful of points out of 807 are enough to move that by an order of magnitude even though they barely move the mean.

### Mean-Shift-Invariant (Segment)

Same terms as the Mean-Shift-Invariant tab (`lag_term()`, same 3x3 layout), but computed on `X_resid` (the `segment_mean()` residuals) instead of the raw levels. This is the diagnostic behind the Segment-ECE row in the Results table below: with the trend already removed, `lag_term()` no longer sees a 60-year monotonic climb, so the `rotate()` boundary wraparound doesn't produce the huge artificial spike seen in the raw-level tab. The remaining large excursions (Transportation around t=600 and t=750, Medical Care near t=800) line up with the 2008 and 2021-2022 energy/inflation shocks, not an artifact.

```{R cpi-trend-segment-ece}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
idx    <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)

seg_ece_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
seg_ece_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
seg_ece_terms_dat <- bind_rows(seg_ece_cov_dat, seg_ece_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn)) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), global = mean(raw)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(seg_ece_terms_dat, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "Segment-ECE term (covariance / variance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::

## Kappa

The default pairwise z-test (`ece.test(..., type = "z.test")`) uses `kappa = "gaussian"` — a delta-method standard error that assumes the fourth-moment terms take their Gaussian values (`k40 = k04 = 3`, `k22 = 1 + 2ρ²`, `k31 = k13 = 3ρ`), with the correlation `ρ` plugged in at its estimated value. We check that assumption by estimating these terms from the segmented residuals directly (`ece.kappa(..., method = "mom")`):

```{R cpi-kappa-check}
#| echo: false

cn  <- colnames(X_mat)
idx <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)

kappa_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  kap <- ece.kappa(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(
    Pair = paste(cn[i], "/", cn[j]),
    k40  = round(kap$k40, 2),
    k31  = round(kap$k31, 2),
    k22  = round(kap$k22, 2),
    k13  = round(kap$k13, 2),
    k04  = round(kap$k04, 2)
  )
})

kable(kappa_tbl, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Under a Gaussian sampling check (iid `rnorm`, same n=807, 50 replicates), these estimators center near the Gaussian reference values with modest spread (`k40`, `k04`: mean 3.0, sd ~0.4; `k22`: mean 1.0, sd ~0.16). The estimates above are far outside that range: `k40`/`k04` reach 15-20 against a reference of 3, and `k22` reaches 4.05 against a reference near 1 for the two pairs involving `Apparel` and `Transportation`. `Medical Care`'s own marginal term (`k04` in the last two rows) is closer to Gaussian at 1.78. The `kappa = "gaussian"` z-test understates the true standard error for these pairs, which pushes its p-values lower than the bootstrap methods (`bs.multiplier`, `bs.parametric`) agree with.

**Fix: test under the null instead of estimating all five kappas.** `ece.cor.se()` forces `ρ = 0` when `rho = 0` is passed, and every kappa term with a nonzero coefficient in the SE formula (`k40`, `k04`, `k31`, `k13`) is multiplied by `ρ` or `ρ²` — so at `ρ = 0` they all drop out algebraically. Only `k22` remains, and it collapses to exactly 1 under true independence for any marginal distribution, not just Gaussian. This is standard practice: testing H0: ρ=0 should use the standard error *at* ρ=0, not one built from the plug-in estimate of ρ. The Results section below uses this null-restricted z-test (`kappa = ece.kappa(X, rho = 0, method = "mom")`, `rho = 0`) instead of the full Gaussian one, so it only has to estimate `k22` empirically rather than assume all five kappas take their Gaussian values. It moves every pairwise p-value toward the bootstrap methods' answer, though not all the way there — `Apparel`'s residual autocorrelation (lag-1 ACF of 0.44) is a second factor that no z-test variant addresses, since `ece.cor.se()` has no lag terms at all; all three tests here (z-test, `bs.multiplier`, `bs.parametric`) assume the underlying series is independent over time, and the bootstrap tests' lag-1/lag-2 correction is calibrated to the dependence `lag_term()`'s own construction mechanically induces, not to arbitrary leftover autocorrelation in the data.

## Omega

`segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` is used throughout this chapter to residualize the trend (for Segment-ECE and the residualized joint tests in Results). It's just one reasonable change-point fit, not a known-true segmentation. We check how well it describes the actual mean-shift structure using ECE itself: `ece.complexity()` estimates $\omega$, the mean-heterogeneity parameter from `omega-estimation.qmd`, directly from the raw data via lagged differences, with no change-point model at all. If the segmentation is a good fit, computing the same $\omega$ quantity from the fitted segmented mean (`lag_diff(X_seg[,i], X_seg[,j]) / n`, the same construction `omega-estimation.qmd` uses for the true mean process) should closely match ECE's own estimate.

```{R cpi-omega-check}
#| echo: false

n <- nrow(X_mat)
cn <- colnames(X_mat)

ece_omega <- ece.complexity(X_mat) |> round(1)
rownames(ece_omega) <- colnames(ece_omega) <- cn

seg_omega <- matrix(0, ncol(X_mat), ncol(X_mat), dimnames = list(cn, cn))
for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_mat))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X_mat))) {
    seg_omega[i, j] <- lag_diff(X_seg[, i], X_seg[, j], k = 1) / n
  }
}
seg_omega <- round(seg_omega, 1)
```

```{R cpi-omega-check-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_omega, caption = "ECE (raw data, no segmentation)")
knitr::kable(seg_omega, caption = "Segmentation-implied")
```

The two agree to within 0.1-2.2% on every entry. This is independent corroboration of the segmentation choice: an estimator that requires no change-point model at all (`ece.complexity()`, built the same way as the correlation and variance terms throughout this chapter) recovers essentially the same mean-heterogeneity structure as the explicit `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` fit. It doesn't make the BIC segmentation the "right" one in any absolute sense, but it does mean the two independent ways of describing this data's mean-shift structure — ECE's differencing-based estimator and an explicit change-point model — aren't in tension.

:::

## Results

We start with pairwise comparisons: ECE and Segment-ECE (ECE applied to the raw levels and to the `segment_mean()` residuals), and naive and residual Pearson correlation (Pearson applied to the same two versions of the data).

```{R cpi-pairwise-cor}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

ece_cor               <- ece.cor(X_mat) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor)     <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)
seg_ece_cor           <- ece.cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
rownames(seg_ece_cor) <- colnames(seg_ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

resid_cor   <- cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

# Null-restricted z-test (rho = 0): avoids assuming Gaussian k40/k04/k31/k13,
# which the Kappa diagnostic tab shows are badly misspecified for this data.
ece_pval_null <- function(X) {
  p <- ncol(X)
  pval_mat <- matrix(NA, p, p)
  colnames(pval_mat) <- rownames(pval_mat) <- colnames(X)
  for (i in 1:(p - 1)) {
    for (j in (i + 1):p) {
      pair <- cbind(X[, i], X[, j])
      pval <- ece.test(pair, type = "z.test", kappa = ece.kappa(pair, rho = 0, method = "mom"), rho = 0)$p.value
      pval_mat[i, j] <- pval
      pval_mat[j, i] <- pval
    }
  }
  diag(pval_mat) <- 0
  pval_mat
}

ece_pmat     <- ece_pval_null(X_mat) |> round(3)
seg_ece_pmat <- ece_pval_null(X_resid) |> round(3)
resid_pmat   <- cor_pval(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)

# Bold any off-diagonal cell whose corresponding p-value is < 0.05.
bold_sig <- function(display_mat, pval_mat) {
  m   <- nrow(display_mat)
  out <- matrix("", m, m, dimnames = dimnames(display_mat))
  for (i in seq_len(m)) {
    for (j in seq_len(m)) {
      sig <- i != j && !is.na(pval_mat[i, j]) && pval_mat[i, j] < 0.05
      out[i, j] <- kableExtra::cell_spec(sprintf("%.3f", display_mat[i, j]), "html", bold = sig)
    }
  }
  out
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Correlation

```{R cpi-pairwise-cor-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_cor, ece_pmat),         caption = "ECE Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_cor, seg_ece_pmat), caption = "Segment-ECE Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_cor, pearson_pmat), caption = "Naive Pearson Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_cor, resid_pmat),     caption = "Residual Pearson Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

Bold marks pairs significant at p < 0.05 (correlation cells bolded when the corresponding p-value is; p-value cells bolded when they clear the threshold themselves).

## P-Values

```{R cpi-pairwise-pval-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_pmat, ece_pmat),         caption = "ECE P-Values (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_pmat, seg_ece_pmat), caption = "Segment-ECE P-Values (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_pmat, pearson_pmat), caption = "Naive Pearson P-Values", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_pmat, resid_pmat),     caption = "Residual Pearson P-Values", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

:::

Naive Pearson correlation on the raw levels is 0.77-0.98 across all three pairs (p < 0.001 for every pair). Residualizing against the segmented mean collapses that almost entirely: 0.04-0.07, with p-values of 0.05-0.26. The pairwise ECE correlation on the raw levels is `NaN` for every pair: `ece.cov()`'s diagonal entries come out negative on these smooth, slow-moving levels, so `cov2cor()` has no valid variance to divide by. This is the same boundary artifact from the Trend diagnostic above (`rotate()`'s circular wraparound), now showing up directly in the pairwise estimator rather than just the histogram. Applying ECE to the segmented residuals instead (Segment-ECE) sidesteps that: 0.13-0.22, closer to naive Pearson than to residual Pearson. The p-values above use the null-restricted z-test (see the Kappa tab in Diagnostics) rather than the full Gaussian one. Under it, Apparel/Transportation still rejects independence (p = 0.032), while Apparel/Medical Care (p = 0.089) and Transportation/Medical Care (p = 0.091) no longer do — both were flagged as significant under the full Gaussian z-test (p = 0.047, 0.073), and both stop being significant once the Gaussian kappa assumption is relaxed. We still don't have a usable pairwise ECE correlation on the raw levels for this dataset — the joint diagonal tests below don't share that instability and are the reliable read.

See the Omega tab in Diagnostics for a check on whether the `segment_mean()` fit used throughout this chapter (for Segment-ECE and the residualized joint tests below) is corroborated by ECE's own segmentation-free estimator — it is.

We run all four tests on the raw levels, and again on `X_resid` (the same segmented residuals used for Segment-ECE above) as a check.

```{R cpi-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat), nrow(X_mat))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

set.seed(123)
results_seg <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid), nrow(X_resid))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{R cpi-diagonal-tests-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(results,     caption = "Raw Levels")
knitr::kable(results_seg, caption = "Segmented Residuals")
```

On the raw levels (left), the Bartlett test and the naive parametric bootstrap, neither of which account for the mean shift, reject the diagonal null outright. The bootstrap multiplier and the mean-shift-aware parametric bootstrap both fail to reject: p = 0.18 and p = 0.41. These raw-level tests carry the `rotate()` boundary artifact discussed in the Trend diagnostic: the last point or two get compared against the 1959 starting level, producing term values in the hundreds against a typical magnitude near zero. We already saw this made the pairwise ECE correlation `NaN`. It also makes `bs.multiplier` mildly trim-sensitive here (p ranges 0.06-0.20 across boundary trims of 0-10 rows, still "fail to reject" throughout but not a fixed number).

On the segmented residuals (right), all four tests fail to reject: 0.34, 0.17, 0.35, 0.09. This is a confirmation, not a new finding. `bs.multiplier` and `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` are mean-shift-robust by construction — they cancel out trend internally via lagged differences and already reached "fail to reject" on the raw levels without any pre-processing. Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap have no such mechanism; fed the raw levels, they see the shared trend and mistake it for correlation, rejecting outright. Once we do the trend removal for them by hand — subtracting a `segment_mean()` fit — they agree with the other two. That fit is not an oracle: it's just one reasonable change-point model (BIC-penalized), not a known-true segmentation, so this isn't "the right answer confirmed by ground truth." It shows that the raw-level rejections from Bartlett and the naive bootstrap were an artifact of the shared trend specifically, since removing that trend by an entirely different route (explicit segmentation instead of ECE's internal differencing) makes the rejection go away. The headline result is still the raw-level table: `bs.multiplier` and `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` reach "no correlation" directly from the raw levels, with no change-point model required. The residualized table is the check that confirms that answer wasn't a fluke.

## Downsampling

At monthly resolution, Apparel's residual lag-1 ACF is 0.44 — high enough to be worth checking whether coarser sampling improves things, and whether the diagonal-test conclusions hold up if it does. We compare monthly against striding every 2nd month (bi-monthly, n=404) and every 3rd month (quarterly, n=269), using the same `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` residualization at each resolution.

```{R cpi-downsample}
#| echo: false

X_bimonthly <- X_mat[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 2), ]
X_quarterly <- X_mat[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 3), ]
dates_bi    <- X_data$date[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 2)]
dates_q     <- X_data$date[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 3)]

X_bimonthly_seg   <- segment_mean(X_bimonthly, penalty = "BIC")
X_quarterly_seg   <- segment_mean(X_quarterly, penalty = "BIC")
X_bimonthly_resid <- X_bimonthly - X_bimonthly_seg
X_quarterly_resid <- X_quarterly - X_quarterly_seg

acf1 <- function(X) {
  X_resid <- X - segment_mean(X, penalty = "BIC")
  round(apply(X_resid, 2, function(v) acf(v, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]), 2)
}

downsample_row <- function(X, label) {
  a <- acf1(X)
  set.seed(123)
  data.frame(
    Resolution = label, n = nrow(X),
    `ACF (Apparel/Transportation/Medical)` = paste(a, collapse = " / "),
    `Bootstrap Multiplier` = round(ece.test(X, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    `Parametric Bootstrap` = round(ece.test(X, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    `Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)` = round(ece.test(X, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    `Bartlett Test` = signif(cortest.bartlett(cor(X), nrow(X))$p.value, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

downsample_results <- bind_rows(
  downsample_row(X_mat, "Monthly"),
  downsample_row(X_bimonthly, "Bi-monthly"),
  downsample_row(X_quarterly, "Quarterly")
)

kable(downsample_results, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Coarser sampling does bring Apparel's ACF down (0.44 to 0.29 to 0.14), but it does not move monotonically toward zero for the other two: Transportation goes from -0.09 to -0.26 to -0.33, and Medical Care from 0.00 to -0.38 to -0.64. Downsampling trades a moderate positive autocorrelation for a larger negative one.

### Diagnostics

Same Plot / Residuals / ACF / Trend structure as the main Diagnostics section above, applied to the two downsampled resolutions.

```{R cpi-downsample-helpers}
#| echo: false

plot_downsample_raw <- function(X, X_seg, dates, title) {
  X_df <- bind_cols(date = dates, as.data.frame(X), as.data.frame(X_seg) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_segment")))
  X_df |>
    pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
    mutate(
      type     = if_else(str_ends(series, "_segment"), "Segmented", "Raw"),
      category = str_remove(series, "_segment$")
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = category, group = series)) +
    geom_line(aes(linewidth = type)) +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Raw = 0.4, Segmented = 1.0), guide = "none") +
    facet_wrap(~category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Index level", color = "Category") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

plot_downsample_resid <- function(X_resid, dates, title) {
  X_resid |>
    as_tibble() |>
    bind_cols(date = dates) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "category", values_to = "value") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = category)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
    facet_wrap(~category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Residual") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

acf_naive_plot <- function(X_resid) {
  par(mfrow = c(ncol(X_resid), 1), mar = c(0, 3, 0, 1), oma = c(4, 0, 1, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
  for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_resid))) {
    acf(X_resid[, i], main = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = colnames(X_resid)[i])
  }
  axis(1)
  mtext("Lag", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 2.5)
}
```

More importantly, the two mean-shift-aware tests stop agreeing once we downsample. `Parametric Bootstrap` (`lag1.diag.psd`) fails to reject at every resolution (0.41, 0.39, 0.48) — stable regardless of n or stride. `Bootstrap Multiplier` fails to reject at monthly resolution (p = 0.18) but rejects at both bi-monthly and quarterly, and does so at p-values on the order of 1e-3 to 1e-17 depending on the bootstrap seed. Both of those are "reject" at any conventional level; the seed-to-seed spread between them is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that this rejection appears exactly when we downsample and is absent at monthly resolution, while `lag1.diag.psd`'s answer doesn't move. We have not identified why `bs.multiplier` behaves this way under downsampling — it could be an artifact of how it re-splits a shorter series internally, a real sensitivity to something downsampling changes about the data (beyond just the ACF, since fixing ACF didn't fix it), or something else. We report it rather than pick a resolution that hides it.

---

Where this leaves us: apparel, transportation, and medical care prices have no known mechanism linking their month-to-month movements. At monthly resolution, every mean-shift-aware test agrees with that: both the bootstrap multiplier and the mean-shift-aware parametric bootstrap fail to reject the diagonal null, while Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap reject confidently, at essentially the same significance level as the two mean-shift-related sector correlations in `labor-productivity.qmd` that *are* real. That's the headline result: naive Pearson and Bartlett can't tell a shared secular trend apart from real contemporaneous correlation, and here we know from domain knowledge which one it is.

The downsampling check complicates that picture rather than confirming it. The parametric bootstrap's conclusion is robust to resolution; the bootstrap multiplier's is not, and we don't yet know why. Take the monthly result as the primary finding of this chapter, and the resolution-dependence of `bs.multiplier` as an open question about the method rather than about this dataset.
